p.src: The story tells how Tripitaka and his three disciples escaped from the Little Western Heaven and joyfully resumed their journey. After traveling for a month, they came to the season of deepest spring, when flowers were in bloom. In every garden they passed, the greenery grew dark and lush, and after a spell of wind and rain, dusk fell once more. Tripitaka reined in his horse and said, “Disciples, it is growing late. Which way shall we go to seek lodging?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Do not worry, Master. If there is nowhere to lodge, the three of us each have our skills. Bajie can cut grass, Friar Sand can break off pine branches, and old Monkey knows carpentry. We can put up a thatched shelter right beside the road and live there for a year if need be. What are you in such a hurry for?” Bajie said, “Brother, how could this possibly be a place to stay? The mountains are full of tigers, leopards, wolves, and other beasts, while demons and specters roam everywhere. It is hard enough to travel by daylight; how could we dare spend the night here?” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, you are more hopeless than ever. Old Monkey is not boasting: with this cudgel gripped in my hand, even if the sky fell, I could hold it up.”

p.src: While master and disciples were still talking, they suddenly saw a village manor not far away. The Pilgrim said, “Excellent! We have found lodging.” The elder asked, “Where is it?” The Pilgrim pointed and said, “Is that not a dwelling among those trees? Let us ask to stay there tonight and continue our journey tomorrow morning.” Delighted, the elder urged his horse forward. On reaching the manor gate, he dismounted and saw that the brushwood door was tightly shut. The elder knocked and called, “Open the door! Open the door!” From within came an old man, dragging a staff of goosefoot, with rush sandals on his feet, a black kerchief on his head, and plain clothes on his body. He opened the door and asked, “Who is making such a clamor out here?” Tripitaka joined his palms before his breast, bowed, and said, “Venerable benefactor, this poor monk was sent from the Land of the East to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. We have just arrived in your honored region, and as night is falling, we have come especially to your residence to ask for one night’s lodging. We earnestly beg your kindness.” The old man said, “Monk, if you mean to travel west, you will never get through. This place is the Little Western Heaven. The Great Western Heaven is still a very long way off. Never mind the hardships farther ahead; even this place alone is exceedingly difficult to pass.” Tripitaka asked, “Why is it so difficult to pass?” Pointing with his hand, the old man said, “More than thirty li west of our village lies a Persimmon Alley, in a mountain called Seven Absolutes.” Tripitaka said, “Why is it called ‘Seven Absolutes’?” The old man said, “The mountain path stretches for eight hundred li, and the whole mountain is covered with persimmon trees. As the old saying goes, ‘The persimmon tree has seven excellences: first, it promotes longevity; second, it gives abundant shade; third, birds do not nest in it; fourth, it has no insects; fifth, its frosted leaves are a delight to behold; sixth, its fruit is excellent; and seventh, its branches and leaves are broad and luxuriant.’ That is why it is called Seven Absolutes Mountain. Our poor region is broad but sparsely populated, and from ancient times no one has ventured into those deep mountains. Every year ripe persimmons fall and rot on the road, completely filling the narrow, rock-walled defile. Soaked by rain and dew, covered by snow and frost, they grow moldy and remain through the summer, turning the entire road into filth. The local people commonly call it the ‘Rotten-Shit Alley.’ Whenever a west wind blows, a foul stench rises from it; even cleaning out an eastern privy could not smell so vile. Now it is late spring and a strong southeasterly wind is blowing, which is why you cannot yet smell it.” Tripitaka was troubled at heart and said nothing.

p.src: Unable to contain himself, the Pilgrim shouted, “You old fellow are most unreasonable! We have come from afar seeking lodging, yet you tell us all these things merely to frighten us. Even if your house is so cramped that there is nowhere to sleep, we can crouch beneath this tree and pass the night. Why must you prattle on so?” When the old man saw his ugly features, he pursed his lips. Trembling with fear yet forcing himself to be bold, he barked a rebuke and pointed his goosefoot staff at him. “You wretch—with your bony, warped face, jutting forehead, flattened nose, hollow cheeks, hairy eyes and shaggy pupils, you consumptive ghost who knows neither rank nor manners! How dare you thrust that pointed snout at an old man like me?” The Pilgrim smiled ingratiatingly. “My good old sir, you truly have eyes but no vision, for you fail to recognize this consumptive ghost. The art of physiognomy says, ‘Beneath a strange appearance, fine jade may lie hidden within the stone.’ If you judge a man by his words and appearance, you will be utterly mistaken. Ugly though I may be, I do possess certain abilities.” The old man asked, “Where are you from? What is your surname and name? And what abilities do you have?” The Pilgrim laughed. “I—”

p.src: When the old man heard this, his anger turned to joy. Bowing, he said, “Please, please come into my humble home and settle yourselves.” Thereupon all four led the horse and carried the luggage inside together. They saw thorny brambles planted along both sides. The second gate stood within walls piled of brick and stone, likewise roofed over with thorn branches. Only farther inside were three tiled rooms. The old man drew up chairs and seated them while tea was prepared, then ordered a meal to be made. Before long, a table was brought over and spread with many dishes: wheat gluten, tofu, taro shoots, radish, hot mustard greens, turnips, fragrant rice, and mallow soup cooked with vinegar. Master and disciples ate their fill.

p.src: When they had finished eating, Bajie pulled the Pilgrim aside and whispered behind his hand, “Elder Brother, this old man refused to let us stay at first, yet now he has served us such a lavish vegetarian meal. Why is that?” The Pilgrim said, “How much could this possibly be worth? Tomorrow he will even have to send us off with ten kinds of fruit and ten kinds of vegetables.” Bajie said, “Have you no shame? You used a few boastful words to trick him out of a meal, and tomorrow we will be hurrying away. Why should he entertain you and provide provisions for your departure?” The Pilgrim said, “Do not be impatient. I have my own way of dealing with it.”

p.src: Before long, dusk gradually fell, and the old man ordered the lamps to be lit. The Pilgrim bowed and asked, “May I ask your honorable surname, venerable sir?” The old man said, “My surname is Li.” The Pilgrim said, “Then I suppose this place must be called Li Family Village?” The old man said, “No. This place is called Tuoluo Village, and more than five hundred households live here. There are many other surnames; only my family bears the surname Li.” The Pilgrim said, “Benefactor Li, what benevolent intention prompted your household to bestow such a fine vegetarian feast upon us?” The old man rose and said, “I just heard you say that you can capture monsters. There happens to be a monster here, so I must trouble you to capture it for us. You will certainly be richly rewarded.” The Pilgrim immediately made a respectful salute and said, “Thank you for your patronage.”

The moment he hears talk of capturing a monster, he becomes more cordial than if it were his own grandfather and makes his salute before anything has even been settled.” The Pilgrim said, “Worthy brother, you do not understand. By making that salute, I have accepted his earnest money, so now he will not ask anyone else.” Hearing this, Tripitaka said, “This monkey always insists on deciding everything for himself. Suppose that monster possesses vast supernatural powers and you cannot capture it—would that not make liars of us Buddhist monks?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Do not blame me, Master. Let me ask a few more questions and see.”

p.src: The old man said, “What more is there to ask?” Pilgrim said, “The land hereabouts is level and peaceful, and so many families live here. It is hardly some remote and desolate place. What monster would dare trouble a great household like yours?” The old man said, “To tell you the truth, our country enjoyed peace for a very long time. But in the sixth month three years ago, a sudden gale arose. Everyone was busy then: some were threshing wheat on the threshing floors and others planting rice in the fields. All were occupied with their work and merely thought the weather had changed. Who could have known that when the wind passed, a monster would appear? It ate the cattle and horses people had put out to pasture, devoured their pigs and sheep, swallowed chickens and geese whole, and gulped down men and women alive whenever it encountered them. Ever since then, it has often returned to do us harm over these past two years. Reverend sir, if you possess the power to capture the monster and cleanse this land of it, we shall certainly reward you handsomely and show you no neglect.” Pilgrim said, “That one will be difficult to catch.” Bajie said, “Indeed it will—difficult, very difficult. We are wandering monks who only seek lodging for one night and will resume our journey tomorrow. Why should we be catching monsters?” The old man said, “So you are merely monks who swindle people out of meals. When you first arrived, you boasted and wagged your tongues, claiming you could shift the Dipper and move the stars, subdue demons and bind monsters. Yet the moment this matter is mentioned, you make excuses and say the creature is difficult to catch.”

p.src: The old man was delighted. He immediately ordered a servant to invite several people—neighbors from either side, maternal and paternal cousins, relatives by marriage, and friends. Eight or nine elderly men came altogether. After meeting Tripitaka, they discussed the capture of the monster, and every one of them was pleased. The elders asked, “Which one of the venerable master’s worthy disciples will go to capture it?” Pilgrim folded his hands and said, “This humble monk will.” The elders were alarmed and said, “That will never do! Never do! That monster possesses vast supernatural powers, and its body is enormous and ungainly. You, reverend sir, are so small and thin that you would not even suffice to fill the gaps between its teeth.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “My good elders, you cannot judge a man properly. Small though I am, I am sturdy; all my refinement is hidden within, as the saying goes, ‘I drank the water used to whet a knife.’” Hearing this, the elders could only agree. They said, “Reverend sir, how great a reward will you require if you capture the monster?” Pilgrim said, “Why speak of any reward? As the proverb says, ‘Mention gold and its glitter dazzles the eyes; mention silver and its pallor makes men foolish; mention copper cash and it reeks.’ We are monks who cultivate merit and virtue. We certainly want no money.” The elders said, “If that is so, you are indeed eminent monks who observe your vows. Yet if you will accept no money, surely we cannot let you labor for nothing. Every household among us lives by its fishponds and fields. If you truly subdue the monster and cleanse this region, each family will give you two mu of good land. Together that will make one thousand mu in a single tract, where you master and disciples may build a monastery, sit in meditation, and practice Chan. That would be better than roaming from place to place.” Pilgrim laughed again and said, “That is even less suitable. The moment we accept land, we shall have to raise horses and perform corvée, pay grain taxes and supply fodder. We shall be unable to sleep at dusk or rest at the fifth watch. What a thoroughly tiresome business that would be!” The elders said, “If you want none of these things, how are we to thank you?” Pilgrim said, “For us who have left the household, no more than a cup of tea and a meal will be thanks enough.” The elders said happily, “That is easy. But we do not know how you mean to catch it.” Pilgrim said, “All it need do is come, and I shall seize it.” The elders said, “That monster is enormous: its head props up the sky and its feet stand upon the earth; it comes as wind and departs as mist. How could you possibly get near it?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “As for monsters that summon wind and ride the mist, I regard them as mere grandsons of mine; and if its body is vast, I have ways of striking it down.”

They have all gone to hide. We are neither their relatives nor acquaintances, much less old family friends. Why should we stay to look at it?”
But Pilgrim was immensely strong. Without permitting further argument, he dragged them into the courtyard with one pull and made them stand there.
The gale grew fiercer still. A splendid wind it was:

p.src: Bajie was so terrified that he trembled all over and flung himself to the ground. Rooting the soil aside with his snout, he buried it underground and stayed as firmly fixed as though nailed there. Sandy covered his head and face and could scarcely keep his eyes open.

p.src: Monkey recognized the monster by the wind. In a moment, as the gust passed, he saw what looked like two faint lamps approaching through the air. Lowering his head, he called, “Brothers, the wind has passed. Get up and look.” The Idiot pulled his snout free, shook off the dust, and looked up at the sky. Seeing the two lights, he suddenly laughed aloud. “What fun! What fun! So this is a well-behaved monster. We ought to make friends with him.” Friar Sand said, “In such darkness, before you have even met him face-to-face, how can you know whether he is good or evil?” Eight Rules replied, “The ancients said, ‘Those who travel by night carry candles; without candles, they halt.’ Look—he has a pair of lanterns to light his way, so he must surely be a good fellow.” Friar Sand said, “You have mistaken them. Those are not two lanterns; they are the monster’s two shining eyes.” The Idiot shrank three inches in fright and cried, “Good heavens! If its eyes are that large, how enormous must its mouth be?” Monkey said, “Worthy brothers, do not be afraid. You two protect Master while I go up and challenge him, to see what sort of monster he is.” Eight Rules said, “Brother, do not give us away.”

p.src: Good Monkey sprang up with a whistle, leaped into the air, and brandished his iron staff. In a stern voice he shouted, “Hold there! Hold there! I am here!” When the monster saw him, it halted and wildly flourished a long spear. Monkey assumed a staff stance and asked, “What quarter are you from, monster? What place spawned you, fiend?” The monster made no reply and merely flourished its spear. Monkey asked again, but still it did not answer and only flourished its spear. Monkey laughed to himself. “So you are deaf and dumb! Do not run—take my staff!” The monster showed no fear and wildly swept its spear about to parry him. They fought in midair, advancing and retreating, rising and falling, until the third watch, with neither victory nor defeat in sight. Eight Rules and Friar Sand could see everything clearly from the Li family courtyard. It turned out that the monster did nothing but flourish its spear in defense, without making the slightest attack. Monkey’s staff, meanwhile, never strayed from above the monster’s head. Eight Rules laughed. “Friar Sand, stay here and protect Master. Let old Hog go and lend a hand. We must not let that monkey claim all the credit and take the first cup of wine.”

p.src: Good Idiot leaped onto a cloud, caught up, and struck with his rake. The monster brought out another spear and held him off. The two spears flashed like flying serpents and darting lightning. Eight Rules exclaimed admiringly, “What fine spearwork this monster has! It is no rear-mountain spear, but a coiling-silk spear; nor is it the Ma-family spear—it is what they call a soft-shafted spear.” Monkey said, “Idiot, stop talking nonsense. Where has there ever been such a thing as a soft-shafted spear?” Eight Rules replied, “Look! It thrusts out the spearheads to parry us, but no shafts can be seen. Who knows where it keeps them?” Monkey said, “Perhaps it is indeed a soft-shafted spear. But this monster still cannot speak. It seems it has not yet entered the human way, and its yin essence remains strong. I fear that at daybreak, when the yang essence prevails, it will surely flee. When it does, we must catch it and not let it escape.” Eight Rules said, “Exactly, exactly.”

p.src: They fought for a long while more, until, before they knew it, the eastern sky began to pale. The monster dared not prolong the battle; it turned and fled. Monkey and Eight Rules pursued together, when suddenly an overpowering stench assailed them. They had reached Persimmon Alley on Seven Ends Mountain. Eight Rules said, “Whose privy are they emptying? Ugh! The stink is unbearable!” Monkey covered his nose and kept shouting, “After the monster! Quickly, after the monster!” The monster darted over the mountain and revealed its true form: a huge python covered in red scales. Just look at it:

p.src: Eight Rules said, “So it was an enormous snake like this. If it wanted to eat people, even five hundred in one meal would not fill it.” Monkey said, “Those soft-shafted spears were its two forked tongues. Let us chase it until it tires, then strike it from behind.” Eight Rules bounded after it and struck with his rake. The monster plunged headfirst into a cave, leaving seven or eight feet of its long tail outside. Eight Rules dropped his rake, seized the tail with both hands, and cried, “I have it! I have it!” He pulled wildly with all his strength, but could not budge it by so much as a hair. Monkey laughed. “Idiot, let it go inside. I have a way to deal with it. Do not pull a snake backward like that.” Eight Rules truly released his grip, and the monster drew itself inside. Eight Rules complained, “If I had not let go just now, half of it would already have been ours. Now that it has withdrawn like this, how are we to get it out? Is this not what they call having no snake left to play with?” Monkey said, “This brute’s body is huge and ungainly, while the cave is narrow. It certainly cannot turn around inside, so it must be crawling straight through, and there must be a rear opening where it can emerge. Hurry to the rear opening and block it while I attack from the front.”

p.src: The Idiot sped over the mountain in a flash. Sure enough, he found an opening and planted his feet before it. Before he had even steadied himself, Monkey thrust his staff into the front entrance. The monster, seeking to protect its wounded spot, shot straight out through the rear. Eight Rules was unprepared. Its tail knocked him sprawling, and he could not struggle to his feet but lay on the ground enduring the pain. Finding the cave empty, Monkey raised his staff, ran around, and shouted for Eight Rules to pursue the monster. Hearing the shout, Eight Rules felt ashamed. He endured the pain, scrambled up, and began thrashing about with his rake. Seeing him, Monkey laughed. “The monster has fled. What are you still striking at?” Eight Rules replied, “Old Hog is beating the grass to startle the snake.” Monkey said, “You living idiot! Hurry and catch up.”

p.src: The two crossed the ravine in pursuit and saw the monster coiled into a heap. It raised its head and opened its enormous mouth, intending to swallow Eight Rules. Eight Rules panicked and retreated at once. Monkey instead rushed forward to meet it and was swallowed in one gulp. Eight Rules beat his chest and stamped his feet, crying, “Brother! This has finished you!” From inside the monster’s belly, Monkey braced his iron staff and said, “Eight Rules, do not worry. Watch me make it form a bridge.” The monster arched its back until it resembled a rainbow spanning eastward over a road. Eight Rules said, “It may look like a bridge, but no one would dare cross it.” Monkey said, “Then watch me turn it into a boat.” Inside its belly, he pressed the iron staff against its belly wall. The monster’s belly flattened against the ground while its head reared upward, making it look just like a Ganbao boat. Eight Rules said, “It may look like a boat, but without mast or sail it cannot catch the wind.” Monkey said, “Clear the way, and watch me make it run before the wind.” Then, exerting all his strength from within, he thrust the iron staff out through the monster’s back. It extended some fifty to seventy feet, like a mast. The brute, fighting for its life against the pain, shot forward even faster than a boat before the wind. It raced back along the old road and descended the mountain for more than twenty li before collapsing in the dust, unable to move. With that, it breathed its last. Eight Rules caught up from behind and again raised his rake to strike wildly. Monkey tore a great hole through the creature and crawled out. “Idiot, it is already dead. Why are you still striking it?” Eight Rules replied, “Brother, do you not know that old Hog has always loved beating dead snakes?” Thereupon they put away their weapons, seized the snake by the tail, and dragged it back behind them.

p.src: Now, at Tuoluo Village, Old Li and the others said to the Tang monk, “Your two disciples have not returned all night. They must surely have lost their lives.” Tripitaka said, “There is certainly nothing to fear. Let us go out and see.” Before long, they saw Pilgrim and Bajie approaching with shouts and cries, dragging an enormous python behind them. Only then did everyone rejoice. Every man and woman, old and young, in the village came and knelt in worship, saying, “Revered masters, this is the very monster that has been killing people here. Now, through your lordships’ good fortune and magic power, the monster has been slain and the evil removed, so we may at last live in peace.”

p.src: Every household was deeply grateful, inviting them here and there and offering thanks in turn. The master and disciples were kept there for five or seven days; only after they had pleaded earnestly and could do no more would the villagers let them depart. Seeing that they would accept no money or goods, every household prepared provisions and fruit instead; riding mules and horses and bearing garlands and colored banners, they all came to see them off. Though the village had only five hundred households, some seven or eight hundred people came to escort them.

p.src: They went merrily along the road and presently reached the entrance to the Persimmon Alley of Seven-Terminations Mountain. When Tripitaka smelled the dreadful stench and saw that the way was blocked, he said, “Wukong, how can we possibly get through a place like this?” Holding his nose, Pilgrim said, “This truly is difficult.” When Tripitaka heard Pilgrim say it was difficult, tears began to fall from his eyes. Old Li and the others stepped forward and said, “Reverend sir, do not distress yourself. Before escorting you here, we had already agreed upon a plan: since your worthy disciples subdued the monster and rid our village of its scourge, we shall each offer our sincere efforts, open another good road, and conduct you safely across.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Old fellow, everything you say misses the mark. You said at the outset that this mountain path runs for eight hundred li. You are no divine host of Yu the Great, so how could you ever cut through mountains and open a road? If my master is to cross, it will still require our own exertions. None of you can manage it.” Tripitaka dismounted and said, “Wukong, what efforts do you propose?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “To cross the mountain as it stands is difficult enough; but to speak of opening another road is harder still. We must go through the old alley after all. I only fear there will be no one to provide our meals.” Old Li said, “Venerable sir, what are you saying? However long the four of you may be delayed, we can easily provide for you. How could you say there will be no one to furnish meals?” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, go and prepare two dan of cooked rice, together with some steamed cakes and buns. Once that long-snouted monk of mine has eaten his fill, he can turn into a huge boar and root open the old road. My master will ride his horse while we support him, and I guarantee we shall get through.”

p.src: Hearing this, Bajie said, “Brother, all of you want to keep yourselves clean, so why make old Hog alone do the filthy work?” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, if you truly have the ability to root open the alley and lead me across the mountain, I shall record this as your foremost achievement.” Bajie laughed and said, “With Master above me and all you benefactors here, pray do not laugh. Old Hog possesses thirty-six transformations, but if you ask me to change into something light, graceful, splendid, and able to fly, I truly cannot do it. But if it is a mountain, a tree, a boulder, an earthen mound, a mangy elephant, a huge hog, a water buffalo, or a camel, I can truly change into them all. Only, the larger my body becomes, the larger my belly grows as well. I must eat my fill before I can do the work properly.” The people said, “We have food, we have food! We all brought provisions, fruit, baked cakes, and buns with us, intending to open the mountain road and escort you. Let us take it all out for you to enjoy. Once you have transformed and begun to move, we shall send men back to cook more food and bring it to you.” Bajie was delighted. He took off his black robe, laid down his nine-pronged rake, and said to the crowd, “Do not laugh. Watch old Hog perform this filthy feat.”

p.src: That fine Idiot formed the spell with his fingers, shook himself, and transformed, truly becoming an enormous boar. Indeed, he was a sight to behold:

p.src: When Sun the Pilgrim saw Bajie transformed in this fashion, he at once ordered the escorts to heap all their provisions together and told Bajie to partake of them. The Idiot made no distinction between raw and cooked, but gulped it all down at once; then he went forward to root open the road. Pilgrim told Sha Monk to take off his footwear and carry the luggage with the greatest care, and asked Master to sit securely in the carved saddle. He too removed his leather shoes and instructed the people to return: “If you have any regard for us, quickly bring more food so that my junior can replenish his strength.” Seven or eight hundred people had escorted and followed them; more than half had mules or horses and sped back to the village like shooting stars to prepare food. The remaining three hundred, who were on foot, stood at the foot of the mountain and watched them recede into the distance. The village lay more than thirty li from the mountain, and fetching the food meant another journey of over thirty li back; with the full round trip amounting to nearly a hundred li, the master and disciples had already gone far ahead. Unwilling to part from them, the people urged on their mules and horses, entered the alley, and pursued them through the night, finally catching up the next day. They called out, “Reverend pilgrims fetching the scriptures, go slowly! Go slowly! We have brought you food.” Hearing them, the elder thanked them profusely and said, “You truly are devout believers.” He told Bajie to stop and eat some more, that he might fortify his strength. The Idiot had been rooting for two days and was just then ravenously hungry. The great company had brought no less than seven or eight dan of food, and, caring nothing whether it was rice or wheaten fare, he gathered it all together and swallowed it down at once. After feasting his fill, he went forward and began rooting open the road again. Tripitaka, Pilgrim, and Sha Monk thanked the people, and the two parties took leave of each other. Just so:
